summary: FlameScope is a web dashboard that turns NASA's microgravity combustion experiments into fire-safety evidence for crewed habitats. It combines 1,018 test records from seven NASA Physical Sciences Informatics investigations (BASS-II, BASS, SAFFIRE-II, ACME BRE, ACME CFI-G, SAME-R and FLEX) into one traceable format. Users pick a habitat (ISS, Moon base, pressurized rover or Mars base); FlameScope ranks the studies, maps every test against that habitat's air and shows what NASA has not yet tested. Specialist AI agents answer NASA's questions for prevention, detection and suppression; code recounts every number from the records, and independent reviewer agents removed findings that were not fair comparisons. The 30 verified findings feed a brief for Moon and Mars missions: oxygen-rich air kept test flames burning longer, yet no cabin material, smoke sample or extinguisher was tested at Moon-base conditions. Every number opens its NASA records in two clicks, and the data downloads as CSV for modelers.
details:
What it does.FlameScope answers one question for mission planners: what does NASA's microgravity fire data say about the habitat we are designing, and what has never been tested? Mission scenarios ranks the seven studies for the ISS, a Moon base, a pressurized rover or a Mars base, with the score split into condition match, fuel relevance and data quality, and an evidence-gap banner. The Evidence explorer filters all 1,018 records, plots them on an oxygen-against-pressure map with the habitat's zone marked, and exports them as CSV or JSON with a column guide. Prevention · Detection · Suppression opens with a Moon and Mars brief, then one summary card per pillar (key points, biggest gap, next test for NASA, implications for equipment and for fire safety on Earth), then 30 findings grouped by NASA's four questions per pillar. Every finding shows how each number was counted and opens the exact NASA records behind it. Ask FlameScope answers questions from the verified findings with an evidence status.

How it works. We downloaded the experimental tables and ISA-Tab metadata for seven PSI investigations and normalized them with Python into one record format, keeping raw values and flagging source problems instead of fixing them silently. A transparent formula ranks the studies per habitat. Insights come from an offline agent pipeline run with Claude: 12 question agents (prevention, detection and suppression × NASA's four questions) propose findings as counting rules, never typed numbers; a checker script recounts every number from the records and rejects overclaiming words; three independent reviewer agents check each comparison for confounding and rejected 3 findings; pillar organizers and one merge agent summarize only the reviewed findings, and a second checker requires every summary number to come from a verified finding. The public site has no AI key and shows only checked results.

Benefits and impact. Engineers and researchers see in seconds which NASA evidence applies to the oxygen-rich, low-pressure air proposed for lunar habitats, and where it runs out: none of the seven datasets burned a cabin material, made a smoke sample or tested an extinguisher at Moon-base conditions, and none ran at partial gravity. FlameScope names the first experiment to fill all three gaps at once. Modelers get the full normalized dataset, and each pillar notes uses on Earth, such as oxygen-enriched rooms, smoke detection in still air and gas-flooding suppression.

What makes it creative. Instead of another chart of past results, FlameScope makes missing evidence visible and makes its AI auditable: agents propose, code verifies, independent agents review fairness, and every claim opens its NASA records. It never labels anything safe or unsafe.

Tools. Python (data pipeline), Next.js, React, TypeScript and Tailwind CSS (web app), Vercel (hosting), GitHub (code), Claude by Anthropic (development assistance and the offline insight-agent pipeline; optional live answers when an API key is configured).

Factors we considered. Data honesty (missing values stay missing, burner-stream oxygen is never treated as cabin air), scientific limits (microgravity only, gas and droplet flames are not cabin solids), accessibility (status shown with icon and label, not colour alone), fairness (compared groups checked for confounding by independent reviewers) and cost safety (the public site runs without an AI key).
